content: Efforts must be made to maintain confidentiality in all aspects of care. It is essential to keep programor facility-level confidential contact details updated to facilitate effective tracing when necessary. When tracing individuals who are not engaged in care, it is critical to assess the risks to vulnerable and key populations. For instance, women living with HIV are at heightened risk of intimate partner violence and gender-based violence, necessitating the proper training of healthcare providers to address these challenges. Understanding the reasons for retention failures, both general and specific to local contexts, is crucial, as these factors are more predictive of disengagement than sociodemographic characteristics like age and sex. Tracing and recall efforts should prioritize individuals who are seven or more days late for a scheduled appointment. While tracing efforts should aim to include all individuals with missed appointments or abnormal results, priority should be given to the following groups: (1) those who initiated treatment within the past six months and have advanced HIV disease, (2) individuals with abnormal test results, (3) those who have not started treatment, and (4) individuals overdue for clinical consultations or laboratory tests. A non-judgmental approach is essential to support individuals in returning to care. This involves reducing systemic barriers and improving interpersonal communication by enhancing the capacity of healthcare providers. The Welcome Back service, established by Médecins Sans Frontières and the South African Department of Health, serves as an exemplary model by combining medical and psychosocial support for individuals who have disengaged from care. Research has identified common reasons for disengagement from care, both before and after initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART). Further research is needed to develop tailored support systems that address these drivers, minimize disengagement, and facilitate re-engagement at various stages of the care continuum. Qualitative research is particularly important to identify the most effective and acceptable methods for tracing and re-engagement, with a focus on disaggregated approaches based on population group, gender, and age. Task-sharing strategies have been recommended to address the shortage of healthcare providers in high HIV-burden settings. Trained non-physician clinicians, midwives, and nurses can initiate and maintain first-line ART, while trained and supervised community health workers can dispense ART between regular clinical visits. Lay healthcare providers, when trained and supervised, can also distribute ART. These recommendations are supported by evidence showing comparable clinical outcomes and reduced loss to follow-up when non-physician clinicians or community health workers manage ART compared to physicians. Decentralization of ART care has been shown to improve access and retention in care. Effective approaches include initiating ART in hospitals with maintenance at peripheral health facilities, initiating and maintaining ART at peripheral facilities, and initiating ART at peripheral facilities with maintenance at the community level. Decentralization reduces waiting times, brings services closer to patients' homes, and strengthens community engagement by linking community-based interventions with health facilities. Point-of-care testing and task-sharing for specimen collection and testing by non-laboratory personnel have been shown to improve access to diagnostics, particularly in resource-limited settings. These approaches reduce the time to deliver test results, improve retention in care, and facilitate timely clinical action. For example, point-of-care infant diagnosis and viral load testing significantly reduce the time to initiate treatment compared to laboratory-based testing. Implementation of these strategies requires adequate training, supervision, and support for healthcare workers, including lay providers. Regulatory frameworks and policies may need to be revised to enable new cadres of healthcare workers to perform these tasks. Expanding human resource capacity and ensuring reliable supply chain systems are critical to the success of these interventions. Additionally, integrating laboratory-based and point-of-care technologies within a centralized laboratory network can further enhance diagnostic access and quality. Research gaps remain, particularly in comparing the performance of newer point-of-care technologies between non-laboratory personnel and laboratory professionals. Addressing these gaps will help optimize task-sharing and decentralization strategies to improve care for people living with HIV.
